source_hash_payload.abstract: Sakana AIは、金融と並ぶ注力領域として「防衛・インテリジェンス」に取り組んでいます。AIが人間には読み切れない量のデータから仮説をつくり、分析者がその仮説を根拠とともに使える状態を目指しています。 今年3月には読売新聞社と共同で、SNS上の110万件の投稿から中国による対日批判のナラティブを分析しました。 この分析では、AIが立てた仮説を記者の取材によって裏付けています。 SNSは一見、世論を映す鏡のように思えますが、投稿の数を数えるだけでは見落とすことが多くあります。たとえば選挙前に支持が厚く見えた候補が、実は党内の動員に支えられていただけだったり、急に増えた反応のほとんどが実は批判だったりします。本当の情勢をつかむには、数十万件の言葉を「誰が・なぜ書いたのか」まで遡って読む必要があります。 AIを使えば、こうした投稿の内容にまで踏み込んだSNS分析が可能になります。今回はそのケーススタディとして、11月3日に投票が行われる米国中間選挙を分析しました。 ▶ レポート全文（PDF）： 米中間選挙のAI分析 — テキサス州上院選 SNSからのナラティブ分析 Sakana AIのナラティブ分析システムは、言説を「誰が・何をして・それがどう評価されるか」という物語の単位で取り出し、その物語を自分の言葉で語り直した人の数で広がりを測ります。抽出した物語は複数のAIモデルが原文と照合し、確かめられたものだけをレポートに残しました。今回の約71万件の反応についても、支持・批判の比率を統計的な誤差幅つきで推定しています。 仮説の深層分析 SNSの中だけを見ていると、言説空間のゆがみに気づけないことがあります。そこで長時間の推論で深いリサーチを行う当社のプロダクト「 Sakana Marlin 」に世論調査、選挙資金、予測市場、報道などの公開情報を調べさせ、X上の観測と突き合わせました。Marlinは複数のAIが仮説を並行して探り、互いに評価し合う仕組みを持っています。Marlinを駆使することで、SNSの内と外のどちらで先に変化が起こったかを、出典つきで辿ることが可能になりました。 テキサス州上院選で分かったこと 約30年にわたって共和党が勝ち続けてきたテキサス州で、今回の上院選は接戦が予想されています。上記のようなAIを駆使して、両候補と両党の州組織によるXへの発信2,042件と、それに寄せられた反応70万5,976件を分析したところ、たとえば次のようなことが分かりました。 共和党の決選投票前にパクストン候補へ寄せられていた「支持」の多くは、党内の指名争いに向けた動員でした。決選が終わると、支持の割合は約5割から2割弱に下がりました。 両候補のリプライ欄で交わされていたのは、二つの陣営が互いに相手の欄へ出向いて攻撃し合う応酬でした。こうした反応の中身と推移を読み解くと、タラリコ候補の相対的な優勢は6月に示され、候補者の資質、経済、宗教、データセンターと主な争点が変化する中で、終盤で僅差の接戦となっていることが分かりました。 X上の言説は、パクストン候補への評価の転変や宗教やデータセンターをめぐる両候補のナラティブとその評価など、世論調査には現れない複雑な動きを示していました。また、両候補者への評価の転換は、Cook Political Reportなどの主要評価機関が判断を変える約2か月前に現れていました。 AIとの協働で行うインテリジェンスへ 上記のような知見は、人間とAIのどちらかだけでは導くことはできないものだと言えます。Sakana AIが先日発表した 「The AI Scientist」の最新版 では、人とAIがともに科学的発見を行う「Co-Discovery」を、これからの科学のあり方として提案しました。こうした人とAIの協働の重要性は、インテリジェンスの領域でも同じだと考えられます。AIは、人間には読み切れない規模の情報から仮説を導き、根拠とともに提示します。それを受け取った人間は仮説を吟味し、取材や追加の観測を行ったうえで判断を下します。AIを駆使して分析し、洞察を導き、最終的な判断は人間が担う。こうしたAIと人間の協働が、AI時代のインテリジェンスのあり方だと私たちは考えています。 テキサス州上院選の分析の詳細は、レポート全文にまとめています。 ▶ レポート全文（PDF）： 米中間選挙のAI分析 — テキサス州上院選 Sakana AI Sakana AIは、AIの未来を私たちと一緒に切り拓いてくださる方を募集しています。当社の 募集要項 をご覧ください。

source_hash_payload.abstract: Redaction summary: As part of this assessment, Anthropic had rights to redact any non-public information in this post. Per our approach to transparency , we had the right to disclose if Anthropic exercised redaction rights, and whether or not any of our findings depended significantly on redacted information. All redactions that were important to our conclusions are described in the report below. Executive summary We agree with Anthropic that catastrophic risks from July 15th models were low, but we think it is plausible that they had crossed their early warning threshold at the time. METR reviewed the “Risks from automated R&D” section of Anthropic’s public August 2026 Risk Report . 1 We conducted this review as part of a high-access assessment of AI R&D acceleration, in which Anthropic shared a private version of the Risk Report along with extensive other non-public data. Alongside this review, we are publishing a holistic assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic . This was conducted by the same METR employees as this Risk Report Review. Overall, we agree with Anthropic that by July 15th, internally deployed models posed low risk of directly automating R&D in key domains or causing acute catastrophic risks from acceleration of capabilities progress. However, the report’s claim that they had not crossed their early warning thresholds relies on contestable judgment calls that aren’t communicated clearly in the public report. While both METR’s researchers on this project and Anthropic’s relevant staff lean toward it not having been crossed, we think it is plausible that it had been, and we believe the public report overall understates the level of acceleration that was occurring. In this review we first summarize our understanding of Anthropic’s Risk Report , including their threat model, early warning threshold and key claims. We then describe our assessment of these key claims and conclusions. Finally, we share details about the process of this Risk Report Review (further details about the process and access can be found in our holistic review ). Summary of Anthropic’s Risk Report Anthropic’s RSP sets two capability thresholds for “Automated R&D in key domains.” Under Anthropic’s RSP v3.4, the Automated R&D threshold is triggered by either of two conditions: Full Substitution Threshold: If they develop a model that can “fully substitute for our entire set of Research Scientists and Research Engineers, at competitive costs (i.e., within a factor of 5).” 2x Acceleration Threshold: If there is “dramatic acceleration” of the pace of AI progress for reasons that likely relate to the automation of AI R&D. 2 This is defined in further detail in the RSP, but the details are not critical to our critique. (Note that although we give these thresholds names for clarity through the rest of this report, they do not have names in the RSP.) The Risk Report argues the Full Substitution Threshold has not been crossed because models are not currently substituting for humans. The Risk Report argues that models do not currently substitute for all of Anthropic’s staff because, despite the fact that Anthropic is highly incentivized to substitute models for research staff as much as possible, research staff still complete work at Anthropic. “[W]e believe it would be clear to us if models were capable of substituting, even at high cost, for the technical work of our entire research staff, and the fact that we do not perform such substitution even when strongly incentivized to is evidence against our models having this level of capability.” Simply put, Anthropic tries hard to substitute researchers out for models, but researchers are still required. They also present benchmark evidence, but we interpret it as less important and more uncertain than this direct observation. The Risk Report argues the 2x Acceleration Threshold has not been crossed as capability metrics and leading indicators show less than a 2x acceleration, with factors other than AI driving that acceleration. The Risk Report describes three primary lines of evidence that they are not crossing the 2x Acceleration Threshold: Limited acceleration in leading indicators: “Our leading indicators point to a picture of meaningful acceleration starting in early-to-mid 2025, though by less than a factor of 2” Limited attribution of this acceleration to AI: “We are fairly confident in attributing the acceleration in 2025 to factors other than our use of AI models, though we also believe that our AI models have been a key factor in the faster trends continuing through the coverage date.” Weak evidence against a sustained acceleration in AECI: Anthropic reports seeing weak evidence of a one-time jump in AECI attributable to non-AI progress rather than continued acceleration. The Risk Report describes the 2x Acceleration Threshold as an early warning rather than direct evidence of high risk. The August Risk Report describes the 2x Acceleration Threshold as follows: “The risk threshold set out in our RSP—a doubling of the pace of progress beyond pre-AI-acceleration rates, attributable to automation of AI R&D—functions as a potential early warning, rather than evidence that the threat has already materialized.” They do not share a precise threshold that would indicate risk was high, but their threat model describes illustrative scenarios: “The threat: We believe that AI models could, in the next few years, have a broad range of capabilities that exceed human capabilities. In particular, most or all of the work needed to advance research and development in key domains—from robotics to energy to cyberwarfare to AI R&D itself—may become automatable. If this is correct, there could be enormous benefits, but these benefits would come with several distinct but related concerns: Sufficiently rapid progress in some areas of technology could change power structures both within and between nations. For example, if an authoritarian regime built a self-reinforcing lead in AI over the rest of the world, this lead could compound into a major advantage in science and technology—which could in turn translate to very sudden and disruptive advances in the ability to wage war, surveil citizens, and/or wield extremely powerful technology over the long term. If AI models develop dangerous goals while heavily automating R&D in key domains, they may cause unbounded harm—up to and including humanity losing control over civilization entirely—by leveraging novel technology and their access to it. If AI can be used to automate AI R&D itself, the result may be extreme acceleration in AI progress, putting a very broad set of risks on the table, including but not limited to those discussed in this report.” Based on these descriptions and conversations with Anthropic staff, we understand the overall risk designation of “low/medium/high” as being about the risk that models at the time directly enable the kinds of catastrophic concerns described above, not the risk that they cross their RSP threshold (though we believe this could have been made clearer in the report). Anthropic concludes the risk from this threat model on July 15th was “low.” Thus, Anthropic concludes risk is “low” overall, since they believe that: their thresholds are unlikely to be crossed, and even if their thresholds were crossed, this may not be sufficient to cause the kinds of catastrophic risks described in their threat model. This is summarized as: “Low. We do not believe our models meet either RSP criterion for this threat model. However, we are less confident in this assessment than we were in prior risk reports, since our most concrete task-based evaluations have “saturated”—i.e., they no longer capture increases in models’ capabilities—and because we are seeing early signs of potential acceleration.” METR’s assessment We find the Risk Report’s argument that the Full Substitution Threshold had not been crossed broadly compelling. The Full Substitution Threshold Anthropic describes is a high bar, and we agree that they would likely have noticed greater progress on automating their research if their models as of July 15th were capable of this. Similar to Anthropic, our confidence in this claim is much lower than it was in the past due to the lack of high-confidence unsaturated benchmarks demonstrating capability limitations that seem critical for automating AI R&D. The lack of such benchmark evidence makes us more worried that alignment, tooling, oversight or elicitation issues are holding back automation despite the models having obtained or being very close to obtaining the required capabilities. We believe the public risk report’s argument that the 2x Acceleration Threshold had not been crossed to be overstated, and believe it is plausible this threshold was crossed by July 15th. Most relevant researchers at METR and Anthropic lean toward the threshold not having been crossed on July 15th, but we think it is plausible that it had been. We believe the public risk report’s conclusion on the 2x Acceleration Threshold seems overconfident, and relies on judgment calls that aren’t communicated clearly by the public report. In particular, we believe the public risk report understated the evidence for acceleration in both AECI and the leading indicators, and also understated uncertainty expressed in the private unredacted report about counterfactual acceleration. Claim 1: limited acceleration in leading indicators. Public risk report Private risk report “Our leading indicators point to a picture of meaningful acceleration starting in early-to-mid 2025, though by less than a factor of 2.” “At our central estimate of the current rate of [redacted] progress ([redacted]×/yr), [redacted] progress rates have less than doubled even if we attributed all of the observed speedup to AI assistance.” METR’s note on this quote: the acceleration rate implied by [redacted]×/yr is 1.97. The 1.97 figure does not appear in the private report; this is our calculation that combines the report’s estimate of the current rate of progress above with an estimate of the historical rate of progress elsewhere in the private report. We believe a reader of the public report would interpret the phrase “less than a factor of 2” to imply an estimate meaningfully below 2; thus it is surprising that the private risk report’s figures imply 1.97. A better description would seem to be “around 2.” METR’s own analysis of these leading indicators, which was redacted from this report, finds a range of reasonable estimates, between 1.3 and 2.8. We have substantial methodological uncertainty about the correct way to measure these values, which we discussed in the full (unredacted) version of the holistic report. As discussed in that report, Anthropic redacted this discussion. METR’s preferred language for the August 2026 Risk Report: “Leading indicators show substantial accelerations, with rates between 1.3 and 2.8, depending on the definition and time period. We are uncertain how these leading indicators relate to downstream capabilities.” Claim 2: limited attribution of this acceleration to AI. Public risk report Private risk report “We believe our internal AI R&D efforts are significantly faster than they would be without AI assistance, but not yet by a factor of 2 (though we are uncertain and measurement is difficult).” “We are fairly confident in attributing the acceleration in 2025 to factors other than our use of AI models, though we also believe that our AI models have been a key factor in the faster trends continuing through the coverage date.” “Overall we expect that end-to-end growth in [redacted] is slightly less than twice as fast as it would be without AI assistance.” “Our central estimates of the speedup of AI R&D progress relative to an unassisted counterfactual are slightly less than a factor of 2 for [redacted]. … we would guess this is more likely to be an overestimate than an underestimate; nonetheless, we have enough uncertainty that it seems plausible we do exceed this factor of 2 overall.” While the first paragraph does express uncertainty about the overall acceleration, the public risk report seems to imply reasonably high confidence that only a smaller fraction of that is attributable to AI, even through the coverage date of July 15th. Meanwhile, the private risk report describes it as “plausible” that the overall counterfactual acceleration attributable to AI exceeds a factor of 2 by July 15th. Based on the evidence we reviewed in our holistic report, we broadly agree with the private risk report’s assessment of the evidence at the time, though directly estimating counterfactual acceleration is very challenging. METR’s preferred language for the August 2026 Risk Report: “We are fairly confident in attributing some acceleration that occurred in 2025 to factors other than our use of AI models, though we also believe that our AI models have been an increasingly important factor in the faster trends continuing through the coverage date. Based on interviews with research leads and informal surveys, we would guess that the overall AI capabilities progress is still slightly less than twice as fast as it would be without AI assistance. We have enough uncertainty it seems plausible we do exceed this factor of 2 overall.” Claim 3: weak evidence against a sustained acceleration in AECI. Public risk report Private risk report “Claude Mythos 5 lies above the historical score trendline by a similar amount to Mythos Preview, which is weak evidence against a dramatic increase in overall model capability trends over time. Based on limited data, Model 2 (not shown on this figure) appears to be around 1.5 points higher on AECI than Claude Mythos 5, with large error bars (a smaller increase than the one from Claude Mythos Preview to Claude Mythos 5).” “Given that not all of our models are trained end-to-end to maximize intelligence per FLOP (indeed, none of them are exclusively optimizing for this goal), there is a question of how many “effective points” we should consider this [AECI] figure to have, and whether the apparent strong linear trend is as reliable a pattern as it appears.” “The most recent and most capable of these four runs … is involved in the training pipeline for Model 2, but we do not think that model's performance is reflective of the performance we expect from later models derived from this base model (which we anticipate to be more significant improvements over Mythos 5).” The public risk report states that Model 2’s score has large error bars, but does not state the qualification in the private risk report that Anthropic expects higher scores from later snapshots of the same base model. In fact, further snapshots of Model 2 did improve on AECI by about the same amount as Mythos 5 did over Mythos Preview. The public risk report also describes finding weak evidence in favor of a one-time jump in AECI at the time of Mythos Preview, but we disagree with their emphasis on this: At the time, the AECI data was only mildly in favor of a jump, and a continued acceleration could not be ruled out. If we reuse the data that was used in the Risk Report, the estimated acceleration is around 1.5x. After the publication of the Risk Report, Anthropic added data from more benchmarks, which estimates an acceleration of 1.9x using the same set of models. We think relying only on the smaller number of models most directly optimized for maximum capability is simpler and more principled, and does not distinguish at all between the two hypotheses. 3 A continued acceleration in AECI would be more consistent with the continued acceleration observed in the leading indicators. As described in our holistic assessment , we think the evidence since the public risk report points in favor of continued acceleration since October 2025. METR’s preferred language for the August 2026 Risk Report: “Given current AECI data, we cannot confidently distinguish between a one-time jump in capabilities and a continued acceleration. However, given the acceleration in the leading indicators mentioned above, a sustained acceleration seems more parsimonious. Two other factors make the current AECI trends hard to interpret: Some models that make up this AECI trend are not optimized for capabilities alone, which makes it harder to interpret how many “effective points” this trend has. Model 2 has not yet finished training, so we expect to see improved performance from later snapshots. Future AECI measurements will likely clarify if there has been a one-time jump or a persistent acceleration.” Despite this, we broadly agree that direct catastrophic risks due to automated R&D from models on July 15th were low. While we think it is plausible, given the above evidence, that models available by July 15th were providing 2x counterfactual acceleration of AI R&D progress, significantly greater acceleration would likely be necessary to enable the kinds of catastrophic risks described in Anthropic’s scenarios of concern above. We also do not believe models at the time could fully automate AI R&D or R&D in other key domains. We thus agree that these risks were “low” for models available at the time. However, as we describe in our holistic assessment , we expect AI’s augmentation of R&D to continue to grow, and we cannot rule out a substantial further acceleration in the pace of capabilities progress over the next 6 months. This could rapidly lead to “high” risks in these areas. Process details Key terms. Shortly after the beginning of METR’s engagement with Anthropic to write an assessment of AI R&D acceleration, Anthropic asked METR to additionally write a review of their August Risk Report, and METR agreed. The exact scope of the review was never formalized, but mutually negotiated over the course of the engagement. COI disclosure. See METR’s Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic . Contract details. See METR’s Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic . Timeline. August 12: Anthropic begins sharing confidential information with METR. August 14: Anthropic shares the August AI R&D unredacted Risk Report with METR. September 18: METR delivers a first draft of its Risk Report Review to Anthropic for feedback. September 22–October 28: METR iterates on the Risk Report Review. October 28: Anthropic gives final redaction guidance for the Risk Report. October 29: Anthropic approves the redacted report. Other disclosures. See METR’s Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic . AEF-1 checklist. See METR’s Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic . The August Risk Report describes the 2x Acceleration Threshold as follows: “The risk threshold set out in our RSP—a doubling of the pace of progress beyond pre-AI-acceleration rates, attributable to automation of AI R&D—functions as a potential early warning, rather than evidence that the threat has already materialized.” They do not share a precise threshold that would indicate risk was high, but their threat model describes illustrative scenarios: “The threat: We believe that AI models could, in the next few years, have a broad range of capabilities that exceed human capabilities. In particular, most or all of the work needed to advance research and development in key domains—from robotics to energy to cyberwarfare to AI R&D itself—may become automatable. If this is correct, there could be enormous benefits, but these benefits would come with several distinct but related concerns: Sufficiently rapid progress in some areas of technology could change power structures both within and between nations. For example, if an authoritarian regime built a self-reinforcing lead in AI over the rest of the world, this lead could compound into a major advantage in science and technology—which could in turn translate to very sudden and disruptive advances in the ability to wage war, surveil citizens, and/or wield extremely powerful technology over the long term. If AI models develop dangerous goals while heavily automating R&D in key domains, they may cause unbounded harm—up to and including humanity losing control over civilization entirely—by leveraging novel technology and their access to it. If AI can be used to automate AI R&D itself, the result may be extreme acceleration in AI progress, putting a very broad set of risks on the table, including but not limited to those discussed in this report.” Based on these descriptions and conversations with Anthropic staff, we understand the overall risk designation of “low/medium/high” as being about the risk that models at the time directly enable the kinds of catastrophic concerns described above, not the risk that they cross their RSP threshold (though we believe this could have been made clearer in the report). Anthropic concludes the risk from this threat model on July 15th was “low.” Thus, Anthropic concludes risk is “low” overall, since they believe that: their thresholds are unlikely to be crossed, and even if their thresholds were crossed, this may not be sufficient to cause the kinds of catastrophic risks described in their threat model. This is summarized as: “Low. We do not believe our models meet either RSP criterion for this threat model. However, we are less confident in this assessment than we were in prior risk reports, since our most concrete task-based evaluations have “saturated”—i.e., they no longer capture increases in models’ capabilities—and because we are seeing early signs of potential acceleration.” METR’s assessment We find the Risk Report’s argument that the Full Substitution Threshold had not been crossed broadly compelling. The Full Substitution Threshold Anthropic describes is a high bar, and we agree that they would likely have noticed greater progress on automating their research if their models as of July 15th were capable of this. Similar to Anthropic, our confidence in this claim is much lower than it was in the past due to the lack of high-confidence unsaturated benchmarks demonstrating capability limitations that seem critical for automating AI R&D. The lack of such benchmark evidence makes us more worried that alignment, tooling, oversight or elicitation issues are holding back automation despite the models having obtained or being very close to obtaining the required capabilities. We believe the public risk report’s argument that the 2x Acceleration Threshold had not been crossed to be overstated, and believe it is plausible this threshold was crossed by July 15th. Most relevant researchers at METR and Anthropic lean toward the threshold not having been crossed on July 15th, but we think it is plausible that it had been. We believe the public risk report’s conclusion on the 2x Acceleration Threshold seems overconfident, and relies on judgment calls that aren’t communicated clearly by the public report. In particular, we believe the public risk report understated the evidence for acceleration in both AECI and the leading indicators, and also understated uncertainty expressed in the private unredacted report about counterfactual acceleration. Claim 1: limited acceleration in leading indicators. Public risk report Private risk report “Our leading indicators point to a picture of meaningful acceleration starting in early-to-mid 2025, though by less than a factor of 2.” “At our central estimate of the current rate of [redacted] progress ([redacted]×/yr), [redacted] progress rates have less than doubled even if we attributed all of the observed speedup to AI assistance.” METR’s note on this quote: the acceleration rate implied by [redacted]×/yr is 1.97. The 1.97 figure does not appear in the private report; this is our calculation that combines the report’s estimate of the current rate of progress above with an estimate of the historical rate of progress elsewhere in the private report. We believe a reader of the public report would interpret the phrase “less than a factor of 2” to imply an estimate meaningfully below 2; thus it is surprising that the private risk report’s figures imply 1.97. A better description would seem to be “around 2.” METR’s own analysis of these leading indicators, which was redacted from this report, finds a range of reasonable estimates, between 1.3 and 2.8. We have substantial methodological uncertainty about the correct way to measure these values, which we discussed in the full (unredacted) version of the holistic report. As discussed in that report, Anthropic redacted this discussion. METR’s preferred language for the August 2026 Risk Report: “Leading indicators show substantial accelerations, with rates between 1.3 and 2.8, depending on the definition and time period. We are uncertain how these leading indicators relate to downstream capabilities.” Claim 2: limited attribution of this acceleration to AI. Public risk report Private risk report “We believe our internal AI R&D efforts are significantly faster than they would be without AI assistance, but not yet by a factor of 2 (though we are uncertain and measurement is difficult).” “We are fairly confident in attributing the acceleration in 2025 to factors other than our use of AI models, though we also believe that our AI models have been a key factor in the faster trends continuing through the coverage date.” “Overall we expect that end-to-end growth in [redacted] is slightly less than twice as fast as it would be without AI assistance.” “Our central estimates of the speedup of AI R&D progress relative to an unassisted counterfactual are slightly less than a factor of 2 for [redacted]. … we would guess this is more likely to be an overestimate than an underestimate; nonetheless, we have enough uncertainty that it seems plausible we do exceed this factor of 2 overall.” While the first paragraph does express uncertainty about the overall acceleration, the public risk report seems to imply reasonably high confidence that only a smaller fraction of that is attributable to AI, even through the coverage date of July 15th. Meanwhile, the private risk report describes it as “plausible” that the overall counterfactual acceleration attributable to AI exceeds a factor of 2 by July 15th. Based on the evidence we reviewed in our holistic report, we broadly agree with the private risk report’s assessment of the evidence at the time, though directly estimating counterfactual acceleration is very challenging. METR’s preferred language for the August 2026 Risk Report: “We are fairly confident in attributing some acceleration that occurred in 2025 to factors other than our use of AI models, though we also believe that our AI models have been an increasingly important factor in the faster trends continuing through the coverage date. Based on interviews with research leads and informal surveys, we would guess that the overall AI capabilities progress is still slightly less than twice as fast as it would be without AI assistance. We have enough uncertainty it seems plausible we do exceed this factor of 2 overall.” Claim 3: weak evidence against a sustained acceleration in AECI. Public risk report Private risk report “Claude Mythos 5 lies above the historical score trendline by a similar amount to Mythos Preview, which is weak evidence against a dramatic increase in overall model capability trends over time. Based on limited data, Model 2 (not shown on this figure) appears to be around 1.5 points higher on AECI than Claude Mythos 5, with large error bars (a smaller increase than the one from Claude Mythos Preview to Claude Mythos 5).” “Given that not all of our models are trained end-to-end to maximize intelligence per FLOP (indeed, none of them are exclusively optimizing for this goal), there is a question of how many “effective points” we should consider this [AECI] figure to have, and whether the apparent strong linear trend is as reliable a pattern as it appears.” “The most recent and most capable of these four runs … is involved in the training pipeline for Model 2, but we do not think that model's performance is reflective of the performance we expect from later models derived from this base model (which we anticipate to be more significant improvements over Mythos 5).” The public risk report states that Model 2’s score has large error bars, but does not state the qualification in the private risk report that Anthropic expects higher scores from later snapshots of the same base model. In fact, further snapshots of Model 2 did improve on AECI by about the same amount as Mythos 5 did over Mythos Preview. The public risk report also describes finding weak evidence in favor of a one-time jump in AECI at the time of Mythos Preview, but we disagree with their emphasis on this: At the time, the AECI data was only mildly in favor of a jump, and a continued acceleration could not be ruled out. If we reuse the data that was used in the Risk Report, the estimated acceleration is around 1.5x. After the publication of the Risk Report, Anthropic added data from more benchmarks, which estimates an acceleration of 1.9x using the same set of models. We think relying only on the smaller number of models most directly optimized for maximum capability is simpler and more principled, and does not distinguish at all between the two hypotheses. 3 A continued acceleration in AECI would be more consistent with the continued acceleration observed in the leading indicators. As described in our holistic assessment , we think the evidence since the public risk report points in favor of continued acceleration since October 2025. METR’s preferred language for the August 2026 Risk Report: “Given current AECI data, we cannot confidently distinguish between a one-time jump in capabilities and a continued acceleration. However, given the acceleration in the leading indicators mentioned above, a sustained acceleration seems more parsimonious. Two other factors make the current AECI trends hard to interpret: Some models that make up this AECI trend are not optimized for capabilities alone, which makes it harder to interpret how many “effective points” this trend has. Model 2 has not yet finished training, so we expect to see improved performance from later snapshots. Future AECI measurements will likely clarify if there has been a one-time jump or a persistent acceleration.” Despite this, we broadly agree that direct catastrophic risks due to automated R&D from models on July 15th were low. While we think it is plausible, given the above evidence, that models available by July 15th were providing 2x counterfactual acceleration of AI R&D progress, significantly greater acceleration would likely be necessary to enable the kinds of catastrophic risks described in Anthropic’s scenarios of concern above. We also do not believe models at the time could fully automate AI R&D or R&D in other key domains. We thus agree that these risks were “low” for models available at the time. However, as we describe in our holistic assessment , we expect AI’s augmentation of R&D to continue to grow, and we cannot rule out a substantial further acceleration in the pace of capabilities progress over the next 6 months. This could rapidly lead to “high” risks in these areas. Process details Key terms. Shortly after the beginning of METR’s engagement with Anthropic to write an assessment of AI R&D acceleration, Anthropic asked METR to additionally write a review of their August Risk Report, and METR agreed. The exact scope of the review was never formalized, but mutually negotiated over the course of the engagement. COI disclosure. See METR’s Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic . September 22–October 28: METR iterates on the Risk Report Review. October 28: Anthropic gives final redaction guidance for the Risk Report. October 29: Anthropic approves the redacted report. source_hash_payload.abstract: METR's time horizon metric has grown exponentially since 2019, along with compute. However, it is unclear whether compute scaling will persist at current rates through 2030, raising the question of how possible compute slowdowns might impact AI agent capability forecasts. Given a model of time horizon as a function of training compute and algorithms, along with a model of how compute investment spills into algorithmic progress (which, notably, precludes the possibility of a software-only singularity), and the empirical fact that both time horizon and compute have grown at constant rates over 2019--2025, we derive that time horizon growth must be proportional to compute growth. We provide additional, albeit limited, experimental evidence consistent with this theory. We use our model to project time horizon growth under OpenAI's compute projection, finding substantial projected delays in some cases. For example, 1-month time horizons at $80\%$ reliability occur $7$ years later than simple trend extrapolation suggests.

source_hash_payload.title: Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026
source_hash_payload.abstract:
Redaction summary:
As part of this assessment, Anthropic had rights to redact any non-public information in this post.
Per our approach to transparency
, we had the right to disclose if Anthropic exercised redaction rights, and whether or not any of our findings depended significantly on redacted information. While we were able to freely share our highest-level conclusions about risk, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions. Anthropic described the redactions as “aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers.”
1
Some of these redactions are themselves challenging to describe clearly without revealing sensitive information we have been asked to redact. We share a table of important evidence we were and were not able to discuss given the redactions in our
process section
below. All redactions that were important for our conclusions are covered by our descriptions in that table or other in-line descriptions in the report below.
Much of the redacted evidence we viewed had multiple plausible interpretations, and both METR and Anthropic researchers have significant uncertainty about how to synthesize the evidence into a holistic picture. This makes it hard for the public to judge this evidence themselves, reconcile it with evidence from other sources, and come to their own conclusions (i.e. this report does not achieve
‘transparency about evidence’
). As a consequence, the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here.
Executive summary
From August 12 to October 29, 2026, METR staff performed a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D.
2
If AI systems started to significantly accelerate further AI development, this could lead to a
sudden emergence of extreme and risky capabilities
.
Anthropic offered unprecedented access to internal data on their AI R&D process, including a variety of metrics on pretraining, reinforcement learning (RL), training compute in each domain, benchmark scores for internal models, AI speedup analyses, forecasts of a future model’s metrics, and interviews with relevant staff.
In our first section,
we share our subjective conclusions about risk
. We now believe that:
As of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. This estimate is given with high uncertainty; we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate.
A majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D, though there is significant uncertainty and other causes likely played a large role in acceleration in late 2025.
The lack of observed bottlenecks or strong diminishing returns means there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration, though, as we say below, we may be missing important bottlenecks.
In our second section we share some of the
key empirical findings from our Full Report
:
Since October 2025, benchmark scores (measured via AECI, Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index) for Anthropic’s models have been growing at an estimated 1.9x the pre-October 2025 rate [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x], implying that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.
We are confident that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scaling of training compute.
Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage causing a doubling in the pace of capabilities progress. Anthropic staff self-report dramatic uplift from use of AI systems in interviews and surveys, although these are challenging to interpret. We were told that R&D is accelerated primarily via AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions, but there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.
We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks which would prevent further capabilities progress due to limits on algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we received more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment.
Some of the key findings that most informed our conclusions about risk were redacted by Anthropic.
In our third section, we describe the
assessment process
:
The scope, setup, and timeline of this assessment.
Details of the information shared with METR.
Details of what information and evidence we were not able to share given Anthropic’s redactions.
Finally, we describe the biggest
limitations
of our analysis:
We could be underestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) evidence that some growth rates have further increased recently; (2) further automation of AI R&D tasks leading to a further acceleration in progress; (3) evidence that AECI growth has sometimes understated growth in real-world impact.
We could be overestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) non-AI factors in Anthropic’s research progress; (2) AECI’s focus on verifiable tasks; (3) reasons why Anthropic’s early growth rate (2023–2025) was unusually low.
The remainder of the report goes into detailed discussion of each of the key components. We include
appendices
with supplemental material.
Our subjective conclusions on risk
Our conclusions on risk.
Independently of this assessment, METR published
an October 2026 article
proposing a set of high-level questions about AI R&D acceleration we believe the public needs to understand to be able to judge loss-of-control risks from frontier AI development. In this section, we describe how the evidence we reviewed in this assessment changed our subjective conclusions on these high-level questions.
Pace of capabilities progress.
A significant acceleration of Anthropic’s overall rate of progress would be surprising, since diminishing returns and dependence on compute scaling mean this would likely require remarkable scaling in other inputs.
3
After reviewing the internal evidence, we still have significant uncertainty and internal disagreements on the team, but most METR staff who worked on this project now believe that, as of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. We would not be surprised if the current rate of growth was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate. We have additional uncertainty in how this acceleration translates to broader and less well-specified tasks.
The 1.9x acceleration [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x] in the AECI trend since October 2025 described below significantly informed this view, but could be explained by overfitting to the benchmark distribution or otherwise be an artifact of the AECI methodology. On the other hand, we are not confident that AECI would reliably let us estimate recent R&D acceleration, since the data points are lagging acceleration in research and are somewhat sparse.
Beyond the AECI evidence, we also saw redacted evidence that significantly informed our view on this question, and made us take this apparent ≈2x acceleration more seriously. It also gave us some indication that acceleration could be above 2x and increasing over time, though we would be surprised if it was significantly higher.
Attribution to AI.
We looked at a variety of factors that could explain the acceleration we observed, including compute scaling, hiring, data improvements, algorithmic discoveries, and resolving other bottlenecks.
As we describe below, we were able to confidently determine that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the rate of growth of training compute. Beyond that, there was not a consensus among Anthropic’s own staff and we did not find decisive evidence. Our overall subjective estimate is that:
The acceleration in late 2025 was likely influenced by non-AI factors.
We investigated a variety of factors which could have contributed to the observed acceleration in late 2025, but details of many of these factors have been redacted.
We guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI.
This judgment is given with substantial uncertainty, but is based on a variety of lines of evidence on contributions from AI and other causes. We believe AI’s contribution has grown relatively more important over time, and do not think the other factors we investigated would explain the sustained acceleration. The evidence of speedup from the usage of AI we describe below also seems compatible with a large contribution.
We illustrate these points below:
Our more detailed estimates for the cumulative and instantaneous effects of AI on Anthropic’s rate of progress in AECI, and at various stages of the model training pipeline, were redacted.
Bottlenecks to further acceleration.
A key concern is that acceleration from the use of AI could start to compound, as the development of more capable models leads to further acceleration. As we describe below, we did not identify any clear bottlenecks (limited inputs that would prevent further growth) or steep diminishing returns to further scaling that would get in the way of such compounding acceleration, though our understanding evolved several times over the course of this assessment, and we have significant uncertainty. Because of this, we believe there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration over the coming year.
Key findings
In this section, we summarize the key empirical findings from our Full Report that we can describe without revealing redacted information (see the
process section
for more details on what was redacted).
Terminology: We describe growth as annual multiples and acceleration as a ratio of growth rates.
We use “acceleration” to refer to an increase in the rate of growth, such that a 2x acceleration means that 2 years of historical progress is made in 1 year.
If AECI’s historical trend was 15 points/year, then increasing to 30 points/year implies an acceleration rate of 2 (it takes 1 year to achieve 2 years’ progress at the old rate). For an exponentially growing variable, the acceleration rate is the ratio of growth rates. If a variable is growing 3x/year, then to make 2 years of progress in 1 year the growth rate must be (3
2
)x/yr = 9x/yr (and acceleration can be written as ln(9)/ln(3) = 2).
Since October 2025, benchmark scores for internal models have been growing at around twice their historical rate.
Benchmark scores of Anthropic’s models, as measured by AECI (Anthropic’s version of the
Epoch Capabilities Index
), have accelerated 1.9x [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x] since October 2025. Put another way, Anthropic appears to have made as much progress on benchmarks in the past year as they did between October 2023 and October 2025 (roughly, Claude 2.1 to Sonnet 4.5):
Our estimated acceleration is greater than that reported in the
Haiku 5.5 system card
(1.7x) primarily because of the inclusion of data on newer unreleased models, explained further below.
We investigated the robustness of these results to different choices of benchmark inclusion, model dating, model inclusion, and benchmark saturation. Robustness analyses find acceleration rates between 1.1x and 2.9x. We would be surprised if the true evolution of benchmark scores (e.g. as measured by an improved version of AECI) showed no acceleration or acceleration above 3x. See our
appendix section
for details.
The acceleration is not driven by an acceleration in the scale of training compute.
We received convincing evidence that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scale of training compute. Further details on this evidence were redacted.
Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage driving this doubling in the pace of capabilities progress.
We have many lines of evidence relevant to AI’s contribution to progress in different parts of the model training pipeline, including interviews, self-reported uplift, headcount, lines of code, experiment usage, and qualitative reflections from leadership. We highlight three important unredacted sources.
First, both METR and Anthropic interviewed many researchers in detail about the degree of overall acceleration in their area of work attributable to AI use (see details in the
appendix
below). Our overall impression was a quite wide range of estimates, but centered around a 2x acceleration. Some quotes, with sensitive details redacted, are in the appendix.
Second, Anthropic also shared data on self-reported uplift due to AI from a variety of sources. The most recent data is from a series of Slack polls, where staff use reactions to vote on their estimated speedup from the most recent model at the time. We consider this to be only very loose evidence, as the responses reflect low-effort consideration. Nevertheless, we observe consistent growth in these self-reports, and very high levels (reaching 12x in October 2026), as shown in the chart below.
Note that individual uplift/speedup estimates do not correspond to acceleration rates. Sustaining a particular growth rate in outputs like model capabilities generally requires a similarly sustained growth in inputs like labor and/or labor productivity to overcome diminishing returns. Achieving a significant
acceleration
in the overall rate of progress generally requires a significant acceleration of these inputs. We thus care most about whether we see a large change in the growth rate of individual uplift, not the absolute level. Our more detailed analysis of what rate of growth in individual uplift might be needed to explain our estimated acceleration rates in key areas was redacted.
Third, we understand that AI is not yet able to make highly significant and fully autonomous contributions to the most important parts of the model training process. However, researchers described significant “signs of life” implying such contributions could occur soon, although with substantial variation in maturity depending on the area.
We did not identify any convincing bottlenecks to continued rapid progress.
We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks in algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data that will take effect in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we got more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment. Anthropic redacted our analysis of a number of specific bottlenecks.
Additional redacted evidence was sometimes hard to interpret, but supports sustained and potentially increasing acceleration.
We investigated a number of internal metrics and methodologies for measuring acceleration in key areas of the model training pipeline. This included evidence of progress on benchmarks and metrics of algorithmic efficiency and overall model strength in pretraining and RL, as well as improvements to compute utilization, inference efficiency and data efficiency. These investigations included attempts to understand:
Different methodological variants of internal metrics. We spent multiple weeks on these investigations, and this is our greatest source of uncertainty.
The beliefs of staff on the relevant teams about key internal evidence and estimates of acceleration.
Whether other parts of the model training pipeline could be biasing our estimates of acceleration, and where adjustments could be applied.
Whether Anthropic could be overfitting to internal metrics.
This internal evidence provided support for there being significant acceleration in Anthropic’s model training pipeline. Some of this evidence indicated that acceleration could be above 2x and increasing over time, but there are significant uncertainties about how to interpret it.
Process details
METR staff assessed how much AI is speeding up AI R&D at Anthropic.
METR staff
4
(2.5 full-time equivalents) piloted a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D, and how quickly extreme and risky capabilities may emerge in the near future.
Anthropic lists AI R&D acceleration as a key risk indicator in its
Responsible Scaling Policy
(RSP). In this assessment, we do not pay special attention to the thresholds set in the RSP. Instead, we try to develop a holistic picture of AI-driven acceleration of AI R&D.
This engagement started in mid-August, and is distinct from the
assessment announced
on October 15 by Anthropic.
Details of the engagement.
The METR staff worked over eleven weeks to independently assess how much AI is accelerating AI R&D at Anthropic. Our assessment focused on three broad questions:
Has the growth rate of Anthropic’s internal capabilities accelerated?
What share of any acceleration is attributable to AI?
Are there important bottlenecks that could slow growth or limit acceleration in the near term?
We were additionally scoped to review the AI R&D section of Anthropic’s August 2026 Risk Report, which we are

We report our best guesses at ways in which we could be misinterpreting the evidence.
We discuss the main ways we could be making mistakes in our interpretation of the evidence. We highlight:
Limitations that result from the structure of this assessment.

Limited access may have led us to miss important context or data.
Despite the access provided to METR, it is clear that staff-level access would enable a significantly deeper assessment. Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied. Being able to read documents on demand, observe internal discussion and debate, and have frequent and diverse conversations would have allowed for a richer view. While we believe we had access to the bulk of relevant information, it is possible we missed important information because we did not know it existed or could not look for it ourselves.
Over the course of our exercise, we substantially changed our interpretation of key data as more context was shared with us, in some cases leading to multiple reversals on critical questions. We believe fuller access would have dramatically sped up that process of proper interpretation, and we think there likely remain points which we may have misinterpreted due to insufficient context.
Acceleration could be higher than this report estimates.
Our best guesses as to how we might be underestimating acceleration:
We may have missed recent further acceleration.
The rate of growth could be undergoing continuous acceleration, e.g. hyperbolic growth. While we do not see clear evidence of this in the AECI trends, there is other evidence that makes this seem more plausible which Anthropic redacted. If growth is hyperbolic, we are likely underestimating instantaneous acceleration and substantially understating acceleration in the near future. In addition, we observe model-level outcomes only after a model is trained, meaning we observe acceleration in effective R&D with a lag roughly equal to the model’s training time.
Automation could be closer than we estimated.
We understand that AI cannot yet fully automate substantial parts of Anthropic’s model training pipeline; however, there are “signs of life,” discussed below. It is possible that automation is close, and leads to very rapid acceleration once human bottlenecks are removed.
AECI could understate real-world capability impact.
We have sparse data on the relationship between benchmark scores and real-world impact. As one example,
ECI scores on math
have not accelerated substantially, but we are now seeing the resolution of Millennium Prize Problems that have evaded decades of human effort. Real-world impacts may be downstream of capability thresholds that models suddenly pass, leading to sudden impacts that are hard to predict.
Acceleration could be lower than this report estimates.
Our best guesses as to how we might be overestimating acceleration:
Non-AI factors could explain most of the acceleration.
It’s possible that the non-AI factors explain all or most of the recent acceleration. This implies we have less reason to expect high future growth or future accelerations.
Acceleration might be limited to well-specified tasks.
Much of the evidence we looked at measures performance on well-specified tasks that are easy to grade automatically or with a language model. If recent models have been growing more quickly on “clean” tasks than on “messy” tasks (relative to historical relative growth rates), then we may be overstating the acceleration in real-world impact. For instance, recent progress may be overfitting to the types of tasks which are included in AECI.
Our acceleration numbers could be overstated if the historical rate of growth was unusually low.
If progress historically was below its normal or natural rate due to temporary factors, this could lead us to overestimate the amount of acceleration. As we describe in an
appendix
, Anthropic models had a lower historical growth rate on AECI than the broader industry frontier before late 2025, which could explain some of the acceleration.

Methodological details on AECI estimation.
We use Epoch’s
public code
to estimate AECI values for each model. We generate 95% confidence intervals via bootstrap by drawing benchmark scores with replacement, stratified by model.
Our underlying data includes the AECI scores of many snapshots per model. These snapshots differ in both dates and AECI scores.
For publicly released models, we include the snapshot that was publicly released and the date that snapshot was available for use by most Anthropic employees. For example, if a model has two snapshots: one available to Anthropic employees on November 10 and one available to Anthropic employees on November 20, and the second snapshot was released publicly on December 1, then our procedure would assign November 20 as the release date. We think there are many reasonable alternative dating procedures (e.g. at first snapshot release instead of last snapshot), which are shown below in one of the robustness exercises.
For models that are never released, we include snapshots that received substantial internal usage and the date most Anthropic employees could use them.
We use the date at which the model could be used by most Anthropic employees instead of public release dates; this allows us to make apples-to-apples comparisons with unreleased models. These in general show slightly higher degrees of acceleration as Anthropic is holding onto more recent models for slightly longer before their public release.
When we fit trends over time we use ordinary least squares with equal weight to each snapshot on the frontier. The confidence interval in the trend estimation only accounts for uncertainty in the AECI scores for each model, and does not include sampling uncertainty over which models are included in the fit.
We estimate a learned breakpoint in the trend, though we exogenously impose that there is 1 breakpoint. We estimate the breakpoint is October 7, 2025 in our main AECI specification. For our robustness checks, we maintain this October 7, 2025 breakpoint to ensure comparability.

A specific concern in measuring acceleration with AECI is benchmarks with many broken tasks, or benchmarks with a fat-tailed distribution of task difficulty. The logistic link function assumes exponential tails of task difficulty; if we instead had a fat-tailed distribution of task difficulty, this would mean that going from 98% to 99% requires more AECI points than going from 80% to 90% (the logistic assumes they are approximately equally difficult). A fat-tailed distribution of task difficulty could cause us to underestimate acceleration; as described above, using cauchit or log-log link functions (which model the last few tasks in a benchmark as particularly difficult) results in acceleration estimates of 2.8x and 2.9x, respectively.
We perform a simple diagnostic test for task difficulty. For each of the 15 benchmarks used for Model 4 in AECI, we compared a model’s estimated AECI against the model’s log-odds score on that benchmark. If the AECI assumptions are satisfied, meaning task difficulty is logistic in a model’s latent ability, then we would expect each plot to be linear. If there are many broken tasks or a fat-tailed distribution of difficulty, then we would expect these fits to be
concave
(we would expect a convex fit if there are disproportionately many easy tasks).
We noticed there are 3 of 15 benchmarks with notably flat or concave fits. When we re-estimate AECI for all models without those 3 suspicious benchmarks, Model 4’s score increases by 1 point, from 178.6 to 179.7. We thus think there is some weak evidence for fat tails causing understatement in acceleration, but the magnitude is not large.

An acceleration in benchmark scores may fail to track acceleration in real-world impact.
Ideally we want to know the real-world value, or potential impact, of each model, not its benchmark scores. If real-world impact is smoothly related to benchmark scores, then we should expect an acceleration in AECI to be associated with an equivalent acceleration in real-world effects.

There are a number of reasons why acceleration in AECI may fail to track acceleration in the real-world impact of model capabilities:
If real-world impact is a convex function of benchmark scores, e.g. if impact depends on crossing a capability threshold, then AECI would understate real-world acceleration. In some domains we have seen a steady increase in benchmark scores accompanied by sudden accelerations in real-world impacts, e.g. impacts on the rate of discoveries in cybersecurity or math (
ref
).
If the benchmarks in AECI cover only a subset of capabilities, and the real-world impact has diminishing returns in those capabilities, then AECI could overstate real-world acceleration. For example, suppose AECI primarily measures a model’s ability to solve formal problems, but there are diminishing real-world returns in that ability; then we might observe an acceleration in AECI without an acceleration in real-world impact.
Overall, we are confident there has been at least a modest acceleration in the growth of benchmark scores. We believe there is significant risk that acceleration in AECI may not map cleanly to acceleration in real-world impact.

Adversarial robustness
We believe this exercise was reasonably adversarially robust.
As this is an independent assessment, it is important for us to do our due diligence and understand how hard it would have been for Anthropic to systematically mislead us, i.e., how likely it is that we could have been led to an incorrect conclusion intentionally.
Adversarial robustness weakness 1: We relied on data from a few Anthropic employees.
Most of our data was received through two technical staff members; however, we interviewed around 15 other Anthropic employees on a range of topics. We did not notice any discrepancies between what our primary contacts said and what our interviewees said. Given that many of these Anthropic employees were chosen by us, not Anthropic, we think this would have been challenging to pull off if we were being given purposefully misleading information.
Adversarial robustness weakness 2: Most analysis relied on Claude.
Claude was involved in many stages of this project, and so in principle could be distorting our perception of the data. We believe Claude was deeply involved in:
the majority of data collection and analysis that we received,
writing a significant share of the documents we received,
the majority of our own analysis.
We did not detect any significant discrepancies consistent with a systematic bias even when checking against human interviews. We suspect this is not a significant risk.
Overall, we think it is extremely unlikely Anthropic was actively trying to mislead us. However, we believe greater access would allow us to increase the degree of adversarial robustness.

We applied

At the start of the project, one participating team member was in discussions with Anthropic about a possible role. They received an offer and declined it. This team member also had equity in a competitor as an ex-employee. As such, we required that all of their work incorporated into the assessment was thoroughly checked

No one working on this project held equity in Anthropic. Our COI policy requires recusal in the case that a relevant staff member holds equity. (None of METR’s staff hold Anthropic equity, but one incoming staff member does.)
We believe there are no other conflicts that would cause a reasonable person not affiliated with METR to have materially less trust in this assessment.
Other disclosures.
Our
process transparency policies
require us to describe both the formal constraints (e.g. redaction and publication rights), and any other factors that may have affected our outputs. To mitigate informal pressures, we generally aim to share enough of the relevant evidence for the public to arrive at its own conclusions, but this was made more difficult in this case due to redactions. In order of impact, from highest to lowest:
Considering impact on negotiations with other companies and possibility of Anthropic retracting access.
These assessments with companies are voluntary and we considered how this output would affect our future ability to do these assessments — for example, if we are too critical of Anthropic for access limitations or making particular redactions, this might make other companies or Anthropic itself less willing to work with us in the future. The biggest effects here are:
We want to avoid disincentivizing companies from sharing relevant evidence with us that they then redact the details of, so we try to focus discussion of limitations from redactions on cases where they impacted our ability to communicate our most core conclusions and uncertainties.
We avoid more detailed process descriptions that would disincentivize companies from doing exploratory collaborations or would make them feel that they need to have everything locked down and avoid changing their mind or discovering new information while working with us. We instead focus on communicating the aspects of the process that ended up having significant effects on our final output.
We made significant clarity edits, particularly to the Risk Report Review, in response to feedback.
Our Risk Report Review went through several drafts, partially in response to significant feedback from Anthropic about communication clarity and reducing the surface area for adversarial misreadings of our report. In some cases we felt this feedback toward METR staff was overly forceful, but Anthropic was receptive to our feedback on this point and we hope to develop more detailed processes and guidelines for this in the future. We do not think the final assessment or the Risk Report Review is significantly distorted by this.
